claim: G-quadruplexes (G4) are polymorphic four-stranded structures formed by certain G-rich nucleic acids in vitro.
source: G-quadruplexes (G4) are polymorphic four-stranded structures formed by certain G-rich nucleic acids in vitro, but the sequence and structural features dictating their formation and function in vivo remains uncertain.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract describing the general nature of G-quadruplexes, supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The sequence and structural features dictating G4 formation and function in vivo remains uncertain.
source: G-quadruplexes (G4) are polymorphic four-stranded structures formed by certain G-rich nucleic acids in vitro, but the sequence and structural features dictating their formation and function in vivo remains uncertain.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the current state of knowledge regarding G4 structures in vivo.

claim: Four G4 conformations were isolated from the hCEB1 sequence in vitro.
source: We isolated four G4 conformations in vitro, all of which bear unusual structural features: Form 1 bears a V-shaped loop and a snapback guanine; Form 2 contains a terminal G-triad; Form 3 bears a zero-nucleotide loop; and Form 4 is a zero-nucleotide loop monomer or an interlocked dimer.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from NMR and CD spectroscopy presented in the manuscript.

claim: Form 1 bears a V-shaped loop and a snapback guanine.
source: Form 1 bears a V-shaped loop and a snapback guanine
evidence: This structural characterization is supported by NMR data and previous structural studies cited in the manuscript (Adrian et al., 2014).

claim: Form 2 contains a terminal G-triad.
source: Form 2 contains a terminal G-triad
evidence: This structural feature is supported by NMR spectroscopy data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Form 3 bears a zero-nucleotide loop.
source: Form 3 bears a zero-nucleotide loop
evidence: This structural characterization is supported by NMR and CD spectroscopy data.

claim: Form 4 is a zero-nucleotide loop monomer or an interlocked dimer.
source: Form 4 is a zero-nucleotide loop monomer or an interlocked dimer
evidence: This structural characterization is supported by NMR spectroscopy and gel shift assay data.

claim: Form 1 and Form 2 differently account for 2/3rd of the genomic instability of hCEB1 in two G4-stabilizing conditions.
source: In vivo, Form 1 and Form 2 differently account for 2/3rd of the genomic instability of hCEB1 in two G4-stabilizing conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic instability assays comparing different CEB1 mutants in Phen-DC3-treated and pif1Δ cells.

claim: Form 3 and an unidentified form contribute to the remaining instability of hCEB1.
source: Form 3 and an unidentified form contribute to the remaining instability
evidence: This is inferred from genetic instability data showing residual instability after mutations that eliminate Forms 1 and 2.

claim: Form 4 has no detectable effect on genomic instability.
source: Form 4 has no detectable effect
evidence: This is supported by genetic instability data showing that CEB1-G21T (which isolates Form 4) remains stable.

claim: Non-canonical G4s exist in cells.
source: This work underscores the structural polymorphisms originated from a single highly G-rich sequence and demonstrates the existence of non-canonical G4s in cells, thus broadening the definition of G4-forming sequences.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the structure-function analysis showing that non-canonical G4 structures cause genomic instability in vivo.

claim: G-rich nucleic acids can form G-quadruplexes, a stable four-stranded structure formed by stacking of guanine tetrads in the presence of coordinating cations such as K+.
source: G-rich nucleic acids can form G-quadruplexes (G4), a stable four-stranded structure formed by stacking of guanine tetrads (G-quartets) in the presence of coordinating cations such as K+ (Figure 1A) (Davis, 2004; Neidle, 2009; Patel et al., 2007; Sen and Gilbert, 1988).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by multiple citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Competitive structural polymorphisms can result from a single nucleic acid sequence when multiple contiguous G-tracts are available.
source: Furthermore, competitive structural polymorphisms can result from a single nucleic acid sequence, when multiple contiguous G-tracts are available (Phan, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and is demonstrated by the CEB1 sequence in this study.

claim: A G4 consensus motif of the form G3-5N1-7 G3-5N1-7 G3-5N1-7G3-5 was adopted based on pioneering biophysical knowledge.
source: Based on pioneering biophysical knowledge, a G4 consensus motif of the form G3-5N1-7 G3-5N1-7 G3-5N1-7G3-5 (where N can be any nucleotide) was adopted (Huppert and Balasubramanian, 2005; Todd et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a historical statement about the development of G4 prediction algorithms, supported by citations.

claim: The G4 consensus motif imposed constraints on the G-tract number (4) and length (3 to 5 nt) as well as on the length of each connecting loop (1 to 7 nt).
source: It imposed constraints on the G-tract number (4) and length (3 to 5 nt) as well as on the length of each connecting loop (1 to 7 nt) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the parameters of the consensus motif, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The G4 consensus motif estimated ~376,000 potential G4-forming motifs in the human genome.
source: This consensus was extensively used to mine genomic sequences, and estimated ~376,000 potential G4-forming motifs in the human genome (Huppert and Balasubramanian, 2005; Todd et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a cited result from previous computational studies.

claim: Recent structural studies unveiled additional 'non-canonical' G4, bearing bulges, strand interruptions with snapback guanines, and incomplete tetrads (G-triad).
source: However, recent structural studies unveiled additional 'non-canonical' G4, bearing bulges (De Nicola et al., 2016; Mukundan and Phan, 2013), strand interruptions with snapback guanines (Adrian et al., 2014), and incomplete tetrads (G-triad) (Heddi et al., 2016; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent structural studies.

claim: Non-canonical G4s result from sequences lacking four G-triplets and thus escape the consensus.
source: They result from sequences lacking four G-triplets, and thus escape the consensus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural features of non-canonical G4s described in cited studies.

claim: A high throughput in vitro polymerase stop assay performed on purified human genomic DNA identified 716,310 G4-forming sites.
source: Recently, a high throughput in vitro polymerase stop assay performed on purified human genomic DNA in the presence of K+ or G4-stabilizing ligand Pyridostatin identified 716,310 G4-forming sites; 451,646 sites did not match the consensus (Chambers et al., 2015)
evidence: This is a cited result from a previous experimental study.

claim: 451,646 G4-forming sites identified by G4-seq did not match the consensus motif.
source: Recently, a high throughput in vitro polymerase stop assay performed on purified human genomic DNA in the presence of K+ or G4-stabilizing ligand Pyridostatin identified 716,310 G4-forming sites; 451,646 sites did not match the consensus (Chambers et al., 2015)
evidence: This is a cited result indicating the false-negative rate of the consensus motif.

claim: The false-negative rate of the initial G4 consensus is massive.
source: 451,646 sites did not match the consensus (Chambers et al., 2015), indicating that the false-negative rate of the initial consensus is massive.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited G4-seq data.

claim: A new G4 prediction algorithm (G4Hunter) emphasizing G-richness and skewness over well-defined G-tracts and arbitrary loop lengths has been developed.
source: Accordingly, a new G4 prediction algorithm (G4Hunter) emphasizing G-richness and skewness over well-defined G-tracts and arbitrary loop lengths has been developed and its predictability (95%) established upon biophysical characterization of hundreds of sequences over an extensive range of thermal stabilities (Bedrat et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a cited description of a new computational method.

claim: G4Hunter has a predictability of 95%.
source: a new G4 prediction algorithm (G4Hunter) emphasizing G-richness and skewness over well-defined G-tracts and arbitrary loop lengths has been developed and its predictability (95%) established upon biophysical characterization of hundreds of sequences over an extensive range of thermal stabilities (Bedrat et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a cited performance metric for the G4Hunter algorithm.

claim: G4Hunter conservatively heightened the figure for putative G4 sequences in the human genome to ~700,000.
source: This algorithm conservatively heightened the figure for putative G4 sequences in the human genome to ~700,000, in agreement with the G4-seq assay (Chambers et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a cited result from the G4Hunter algorithm.

claim: Among a set of validated G4-forming variant sequences of the human minisatellite CEB25, only the G4s with short loops preferentially containing pyrimidine were capable of inducing genomic instability in S. cerevisiae.
source: Relevant to the present study, we recently showed that, among a set of validated G4-forming variant sequences of the human minisatellite CEB25, only the G4s with short loops preferentially containing pyrimidine were capable of inducing genomic instability in the eukaryotic model organism S. cerevisiae (Piazza et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a cited result from the authors' previous work.

claim: Only a subset of G4-forming sequences actually formed and/or exerted a biological effect in S. cerevisiae.
source: These results demonstrated that only a subset of G4-forming sequences actually formed and/or exerted a biological effect; in this case, the ability to interfere with leading strand DNA replication (Lopes et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the authors' previous experimental work.

claim: The unstable CEB25-G4 motif variant bearing short loops matched the G4 consensus.
source: While the unstable CEB25-G4 motif variant bearing short loops matched the G4 consensus (Piazza et al., 2015)
evidence: This is a cited observation from previous work.

claim: The human minisatellite CEB1 was unstable despite the lack of a consensus G4 motif.
source: we also previously reported that the human minisatellite CEB1 was similarly unstable despite the lack of a consensus G4 motif (Lopes et al., 2011; Piazza et al., 2010, 2012; Ribeyre et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a cited observation from the authors' previous work.

claim: The CEB1 motif was forming a mixture of several G4 conformations in solution that could not be individually resolved in the first biophysical study.
source: Our first biophysical study suggested that the CEB1 motif was forming a mixture of several G4 conformations in solution that could not be individually resolved (Ribeyre et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a cited observation from previous work.

claim: The CEB1 instability depends on its ability to form G4(s) in vivo.
source: We previously showed that the CEB1 instability depends on its ability to form G4(s) in vivo by simultaneously mutating the G-sextet and each G triplet (CEB1-Gmut in Table 1) (Ribeyre et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a cited result from previous genetic experiments.

claim: CEB1-WT-20 and CEB1-WT-25 alleles were stable in WT cells (0% and 2.5% instability, respectively).
source: These synthetic alleles were stable in WT cells (0% and 2.5% instability, respectively)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Southern blot analysis.

claim: CEB1-WT-20 and CEB1-WT-25 alleles were significantly unstable in Phen-DC3-treated WT cells (10.9% and 12% instability, respectively).
source: significantly unstable both in Phen-DC3-treated WT cells (10.9% and 12% instability, respectively)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Southern blot analysis.

claim: CEB1-WT-20 and CEB1-WT-25 alleles were significantly unstable in the pif1Δ mutant (25.6% and 59.1% instability, respectively).
source: significantly unstable both in Phen-DC3-treated WT cells (10.9% and 12% instability, respectively) and in the pif1Δ mutant (25.6% and 59.1% instability, respectively) (Table 1 and Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Southern blot analysis.

claim: The CEB1-G3T variant exhibited significant instability upon Phen-DC3 treatment and PIF1 deletion (8.9% and 20.0%).
source: Clearly, the CEB1-G3T variant exhibited a significant instability upon Phen-DC3 treatment and PIF1 deletion (8.9% and 20.0%) (Table 1 and Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Southern blot analysis.

claim: The CEB1-G17T and CEB1-G21T alleles remained stable in both Phen-DC3 and pif1Δ assays (≤1.1% rearrangements).
source: In contrast, the CEB1-G17T and CEB1-G21T alleles remained stable in both assays (≤1.1% rearrangements), significantly different from CEB1-WT (Table 1 and Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Southern blot analysis.

claim: The G16-18 and G20-22 triplets are critical for CEB1 instability.
source: Thus, the G16-18 and G20-22 triplets are critical for CEB1 instability while G2-4 is dispensable (see below).
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the mutagenesis data showing that mutations in G17 and G21 abolish instability.

claim: G2-4 is dispensable for CEB1 instability.
source: Thus, the G16-18 and G20-22 triplets are critical for CEB1 instability while G2-4 is dispensable (see below).
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the mutagenesis data showing that the G3T mutation does not reduce instability.

claim: Substitution of the A19 loop by a Thymine significantly increased the genomic instability of CEB1 in Phen-DC3-treated WT cells (from 10.9% to 29.7%).
source: As expected, this single nucleotide substitution significantly increased the genomic instability of CEB1 in the Phen-DC3-treated WT cells (from 10.9% to 29.7%)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Substitution of the A19 loop by a Thymine significantly increased the genomic instability of CEB1 in the pif1Δ strain (from 25.6% to 50.0%).
source: this single nucleotide substitution significantly increased the genomic instability of CEB1 in the Phen-DC3-treated WT cells (from 10.9% to 29.7%) and in the pif1Δ strain (from 25.6% to 50.0%) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Extending the size of the A19 loop in CEB1-A19TT and CEB1-A19TTT gradually reduced the minisatellite instability to low or background levels.
source: Furthermore, extending the size of this loop in CEB1-A19TT and CEB1-A19TTT gradually reduced the minisatellite instability to low or background levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: G4s bearing short (≤3 nt) pyrimidine-containing loops are more prone to trigger genomic instability.
source: Hence, we confirmed with the complex CEB1 sequence that G4s bearing short (≤3 nt) pyrimidine-containing loops are more prone to trigger genomic instability.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the loop length experiments and is consistent with previous findings.

claim: The G(9-10,14)T, G(10-13)T, G(11,13)T and G13T constructs clearly abolished CEB1 instability in both Phen-DC3 and pif1Δ conditions.
source: Most dramatically, the G(9-10,14)T, G(10-13)T, G(11,13)T and G13T constructs clearly abolished CEB1 instability in both conditions (Table 1 and Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Southern blot analysis.

claim: The CEB1-G(11-12)T allele remained stable in Phen-DC3-treated WT cells.
source: The CEB1-G(11-12)T allele, only assayed in Phen-DC3-treated WT cells, also remained stable (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Southern blot analysis.

claim: The G(9-10)T, G(9-11)T and G11T mutations had no effect on CEB1 instability in both Phen-DC3 and pif1Δ conditions.
source: In contrast, the G(9-10)T, G(9-11)T and G11T mutations had no effect in both conditions (Table 1 and Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Southern blot analysis.

claim: The CEB1-G14T allele exhibited an intermediate instability, significantly lower than CEB1-WT in both conditions, yet not abolished.
source: The CEB1-G14T allele exhibited an intermediate instability, significantly lower than CEB1-WT in both conditions, yet not abolished (Table 1 and Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Southern blot analysis.

claim: G12T exhibited a significantly higher level of instability than CEB1-WT in Phen-DC3-treated WT cells (19.6 vs. 12.0%, p-value=0.05).
source: Finally, G12T was unusual since it exhibited a significantly higher level of instability than CEB1-WT in Phen-DC3-treated WT cells (19.6 vs. 12.0%, p-value=0.05)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Southern blot analysis with statistical comparison.

claim: G12T exhibited a lower instability than CEB1-WT in the absence of Pif1 (10.2 vs. 59.1%, p-value<0.01).
source: and a lower instability in the absence of Pif1 (10.2 vs. 59.1%, p-value<0.01) (Table 1 and Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Southern blot analysis with statistical comparison.

claim: Not all the Gs in the G-sextet contribute to CEB1 instability.
source: These results show that not all the Gs in the G-sextet contribute to CEB1 instability.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the differential effects of mutations within the G-sextet.

claim: All the mutations that disrupt the G12-14 triplet either strongly reduced or abolished CEB1 instability.
source: With the exception of the G12T substitution, which is discussed below, all the mutations that disrupt the G12-14 triplet either strongly reduced or abolished CEB1 instability.
evidence: This is a summary of the mutagenesis data for the G12-14 region.

claim: Mutations of G9-11 triplets had either no or modest effects on CEB1 instability.
source: In contrast, mutations of G9-11 triplets had either no or modest effects on CEB1 instability.
evidence: This is a summary of the mutagenesis data for the G9-11 region.

claim: Critical for CEB1 instability is the presence of a G-triplet in the G-sextet, immediately contiguous with the two other essential G16-18 and G20-22 triplets.
source: Hence, critical for CEB1 instability is the presence of a G-triplet in the G-sextet, immediately contiguous with the two other essential G16-18 and G20-22 triplets.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the mutagenesis data showing the importance of G12-14.

claim: Shifting the G12-14 triplet by a single nucleotide away from G20-22 significantly reduced or abolished CEB1 instability.
source: Shifting this G12-14 triplet by a single nucleotide away from G20-22 (in CEB1-G(9-10,14)T and CEB1-G14T) significantly reduced or abolished CEB1 instability, consistent with the stabilizing effect of increased loop length.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and is consistent with the loop length effects.

claim: Three G-triplets (G12-14, G16-18, and G20-22) separated by single nucleotide loops are necessary for sustaining most of the CEB1 instability.
source: In conclusion, our mutational analysis identified three G-triplets (G12-14, G16-18, and G20-22) separated by single nucleotide loops as necessary for sustaining most of the CEB1 instability.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the comprehensive mutagenesis analysis.

claim: The distant fourth G2-4 triplet is dispensable for CEB1 instability.
source: Since the distant fourth G2-4 triplet is dispensable for CEB1 instability, the sequence causing the bulk of CEB1 instability escapes the G3N1-7G3N1-7G3N1-7G3 consensus.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis data showing that G3T does not reduce instability.

claim: The sequence causing the bulk of CEB1 instability escapes the G3N1-7G3N1-7G3N1-7G3 consensus.
source: Since the distant fourth G2-4 triplet is dispensable for CEB1 instability, the sequence causing the bulk of CEB1 instability escapes the G3N1-7G3N1-7G3N1-7G3 consensus.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the finding that only three G-triplets are required, not four.

claim: The CEB1-G(24-25)T and CEB1-G25T alleles exhibited a significant ~3 fold decrease of instability compared to CEB1-WT upon Phen-DC3 treatment (3.6% and 4.2% compared to 12%).
source: Strikingly, the CEB1-G(24-25)T and CEB1-G25T alleles exhibited a significant ~3 fold decrease of instability compared to CEB1-WT upon Phen-DC3 treatment (3.6% and 4.2% compared to 12%)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Southern blot analysis.

claim: The CEB1-G(24-25)T and CEB1-G25T alleles exhibited a significant ~3 fold decrease of instability compared to CEB1-WT upon PIF1 deletion (9.4% and 16.1% compared to 59.1%).
source: and PIF1 deletion (9.4% and 16.1% compared to 59.1%) (Table 1 and Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Southern blot analysis.

claim: The CEB1-G(31-32)T and CEB1-G(34-35)T mutants were as unstable as the similarly sized CEB1-WT arrays in both Phen-DC3 and pif1Δ conditions.
source: In contrast, for both conditions, the CEB1-G(31-32)T and CEB1-G(34-35)T mutants were as unstable as the similarly sized CEB1-WT arrays (Table 1 and Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Southern blot analysis.

claim: The G24-25 doublet is important in CEB1 instability, contributing to ~2/3rd of the CEB1-WT instability.
source: These results demonstrate the importance of the G24-25 doublet in CEB1 instability, contributing to ~2/3rd of the CEB1-WT instability.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the quantitative analysis of the G24-25 mutants.

claim: Combining the G(24-25)T mutations with the G-sextet G(9-10)T, G(9-11)T or G14T mutations consistently abolished the remaining G24-25-independent instability (≤1.5%) in Phen-DC3-treated cells.
source: In all cases, the remaining G24-25-independent instability was consistently abolished (≤1.5%) in the Phen-DC3-treated cells (Table 1 and Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Southern blot analysis.

claim: In the absence of Pif1, the G(9-11, 25)T construct abolished instability (<0.5%), significantly less than the 16.1% observed in the single G25T mutant.
source: Accordingly, in the absence of Pif1, the instability was also abolished in the G(9-11, 25)T construct (<0.5%), significantly less than the 16.1% observed in the single G25T mutant (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Southern blot analysis.

claim: The remaining G24-25-independent CEB1 instability requires the G-sextet in both Phen-DC3 and pif1Δ conditions.
source: These results indicate that the remaining G24-25-independent CEB1 instability requires the G-sextet in both conditions.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the double mutant analysis.

claim: In Phen-DC3-treated WT cells, CEB1-G(3,24–25)T behaved like CEB1-G(24-25)T (3.7% vs. 3.6%).
source: In Phen-DC3-treated WT cells, it behaved like CEB1-G(24-25)T (3.7% vs. 3.6%) (Table 1 and Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Southern blot analysis.

claim: In Pif1-deficient cells, the G3T mutation in CEB1-G(3,24–25)T ablated the remaining G24-25-independent instability (1.1% vs. 9.4% or 16.1% in G(24-25)T and G25T, respectively, p-values<0.05).
source: Differently, in Pif1-deficient cells this additional G3T mutation ablated the remaining G24-25-independent instability (1.1% vs. 9.4% or 16.1% in G(24-25)T and G25T, respectively, p-values<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Southern blot analysis with statistical comparison.

claim: In the absence of Pif1, but not in the WT+Phen-DC3 context, the G24-25-independent instability uniquely relies on the distant G2-4 triplet.
source: These data indicate that in the absence of Pif1, but not in in the WT+Phen-DC3 context, the G24-25-independent instability uniquely relies on the distant G2-4 triplet.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the differential behavior of the G(3,24-25)T mutant in the two conditions.

claim: Multiple G4s contribute to CEB1 instability, and these G4s are not necessarily the same in the presence of the Phen-DC3 ligand or in the absence of the Pif1 helicase.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that multiple G4s contribute to CEB1 instability, and these G4s are not necessarily the same in the presence of the Phen-DC3 ligand or in the absence of the Pif1 helicase (see Discussion).
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the differential G-tract requirements in the two conditions.

claim: One set of G-tracts (G3AG3AG3TG2) accounts for ~2/3rd of the instability in both G4-stabilizing conditions and uniquely involves the G24-25-doublet.
source: One (G3AG3AG3TG2) accounts for ~2/3rd of the instability in both G4-stabilizing conditions: it uniquely involves the G24-25-doublet.
evidence: This is a summary of the mutagenesis data identifying the G-tracts required for instability.

claim: Another set of G-tracts (G6AG3AG3) accounts for the remaining ~1/3rd of the instability in the Phen-DC3 context only and uniquely involves the entire G9-14-sextet and lacks a third non-null loop.
source: Another (G6AG3AG3) accounts for the remaining ~1/3rd of the instability in the Phen-DC3 context only: it uniquely involves the entire G9-14-sextet and lacks a third non-null loop.
evidence: This is a summary of the mutagenesis data identifying the G-tracts required for instability in the Phen-DC3 context.

claim: A third set of G-tracts (G3N4G6AG3AG3) accounts for the remaining ~1/3rd of the instability in the pif1Δ context only and uniquely involves the distant G2-4 triplet separated from the rest of the G-tracts by 4 nts.
source: The last one (G3N4G6AG3AG3) accounts for the remaining ~1/3rd of the instability in the pif1Δ context only: it uniquely involves the distant G2-4 triplet separated from the rest of the G-tracts by 4 nts.
evidence: This is a summary of the mutagenesis data identifying the G-tracts required for instability in the pif1Δ context.

claim: Imino proton spectra of the CEB1 motif (39-nt) evidently indicated the formation of multiple G4s, but no well-defined conformation could be identified.
source: Imino proton spectra of the CEB1 motif (39-nt, Figure 4A,B) or its G-rich segment (25-nt, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) evidently indicated the formation of multiple G4s, but no well-defined conformation could be identified.
evidence: This is supported by NMR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Four truncated sequences representing 4 combinations of G tracts each exhibited a clear NMR spectra corresponding to intramolecular G4s, named Forms 1 to 4.
source: Consequently, we truncated the sequence to represent 4 combinations of G tracts, the structural characteristics of which were assessed using NMR and circular dichroism (CD) spectroscopy. Each of the sequence exhibited a clear NMR spectra corresponding to intramolecular G4s, named Forms 1 to 4 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by NMR and CD spectroscopy data shown in Figure 4.

claim: CD spectra of Forms 1-4 exhibited a positive peak at 260 nm and a negative peak at 240 nm, characteristic of a parallel-stranded G4.
source: CD spectra of these forms exhibited a positive peak at 260 nm and a negative peak at 240 nm, characteristic of a parallel-stranded G4 (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2) (Wieland and Hartig, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by CD spectroscopy data and cited knowledge about G4 CD signatures.

claim: All four G4 conformations isolated from the CEB1 motif exhibited non-canonical structural features.
source: Interestingly, all these conformations exhibited non-canonical structural features.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the structural characterization of Forms 1-4.

claim: Form 1 was previously shown to be a parallel, single-nucleotide loop G4 bearing an interrupted strand and a snapback guanine with a V-shaped loop.
source: Form 1 was previously shown to be a parallel, single-nucleotide loop G4 bearing an interrupted strand and a snapback guanine with a V-shaped loop. Form 1 can exist as a monomer and dimerize at high concentration (Adrian et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a cited result from previous structural work.

claim: Form 1 can exist as a monomer and dimerize at high concentration.
source: Form 1 can exist as a monomer and dimerize at high concentration (Adrian et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a cited result from previous structural work.

claim: Form 2 can be a G4 resembling Form 1 but lacks the G9 or G10 snapback guanine, leaving a vacant guanine in the lowermost quartet.
source: Form 2 can be a G4 resembling Form 1 but lacks the G9 or G10 snapback guanine, leaving a vacant guanine in the lowermost quartet.
evidence: This is a structural characterization based on NMR data and comparison with Form 1.

claim: G-triad-bearing G4s have recently been reported.
source: Such G-triad-bearing G4s have recently been reported by us and others (Heddi et al., 2016; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent structural studies.

claim: Form 3 can fold into a monomeric parallel G4 with an unusual zero-nt loop and two 1-nt propeller loops.
source: Form 3 that incorporates only a G-sextet and two G-triplets separated by a single residue can fold into a monomeric parallel G4 with an unusual zero-nt loop and two 1-nt propeller loops.
evidence: This is a structural characterization based on NMR and CD data.

claim: Form 4 can fold into a parallel G4 containing a 4-nt, a zero-nt, and a 1-nt loops.
source: Finally, Form 4 can fold into a parallel G4 containing a 4-nt, a zero-nt, and a 1-nt loops.
evidence: This is a structural characterization based on NMR and CD data.

claim: Form 4 is in equilibrium between an interlocked dimeric G4 and a monomeric G4, depending on the salt and DNA strand concentration.
source: Depending on the salt and DNA strand concentration, Form 4 is in equilibrium between an interlocked dimeric G4 and a monomeric G4 (Appendix 1, Figure 4—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by NMR spectroscopy and gel shift assay data shown in the supplementary figures.

claim: The CEB1 motif is able to fold into several non-canonical G4s in vitro.
source: Altogether, the biophysical analyses of the highly contiguous CEB1 G-rich sub-motifs demonstrate that the CEB1 motif is able to fold into several non-canonical G4s in vitro.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the comprehensive biophysical characterization of Forms 1-4.

claim: Form 4 is not involved in CEB1 instability as the CEB1-G21T mutant remains perfectly stable in all conditions.
source: Clearly, Form 4 is not involved in CEB1 instability as the CEB1-G21T mutant remains perfectly stable in all conditions.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the genetic instability data for the G21T mutant.

claim: Form 1 + 2 accounted for 2/3rd of the instability in both Phen-DC3 and pif1Δ contexts.
source: Form 1 + 2 accounted for 2/3rd of the instability in both contexts (Figures 3D, 5A and B).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the genetic instability data for mutants that isolate Forms 1 and 2.

claim: Form 2 is sufficient to cause instability in the presence of Phen-DC3.
source: Further isolation of Form 2 from Form 1 (in CEB1-G(3,9–11)T and -G(9-11)T) showed that Form 2 is sufficient in the presence of Phen-DC3
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the genetic instability data for mutants that isolate Form 2.

claim: Form 1 preferentially causes instability in the absence of Pif1.
source: while Form 1 preferentially causes instability in the absence of Pif1 (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from comparing the instability of mutants that allow Form 1 vs. those that isolate Form 2 in the pif1Δ context.

claim: The 0-nt containing loop Form 3 contributed to the remaining third of instability only in the Phen-DC3 context.
source: The 0-nt containing loop Form 3 contributed to the remaining third of instability only in the Phen-DC3 context (Figures 3D, 5A and B).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the genetic instability data for mutants that isolate Form 3.

claim: All the forms inducing CEB1 instability (Form 1, 2, and 3) bear single/zero nucleotide loops.
source: Consistent with this preferential folding bias, it is remarkable that all the forms inducing CEB1 instability (Form 1, 2, and 3) bear single/zero nucleotide loops (Figure 4A)
evidence: This is an observation based on the structural characterization of the forms.

claim: Increasing a loop by a single nucleotide has a profound effect on the array instability.
source: and that increasing a loop by a single nucleotide has such a profound effect on the array instability (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data on loop length variants.

claim: The G11T mutant (Form 1 + 2) has a Tm similar to CEB1-WT.
source: According to the G4 forms, the G11T mutant (Form 1 + 2) has a Tm similar to CEB1-WT
evidence: This is supported by UV-melting data reported in Table 1.

claim: Form 2 alone (G(3,9–11)T), Form 3 (G(3,G24-25)T) and Form 4 (G21T) exhibit low Tms (46°C or less).
source: while all the other forms, namely Form 2 alone (G(3,9–11)T), Form 3 (G(3,G24-25)T) and Form 4 (G21T) exhibit low Tms (46°C or less) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by UV-melting data reported in Table 1 and Figure 5A.

claim: A clear correlation can be established between the Tm of all the variants and their level of instability in the WT+Phen-DC3 and pif1Δ contexts.
source: Although a clear correlation can be established in both contexts, few notable outliers were observed, especially upon Phen-DC3 treatment (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Form 4 did not induce instability despite a Tm similar to Form 2 and higher than Form 3.
source: Among the outliers, we noted that Form 4 did not induced instability despite a Tm similar to Form 2 and higher than Form 3 (Figures 5A and 6A).
evidence: This is an observation based on comparing Tm values and instability data.

claim: A single loop ≥4 nt was sufficient to stabilize the array independently of the Tm.
source: This is consistent with our previous findings that a single loop ≥4 nt was sufficient to stabilize the array independently of the Tm (Piazza et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a cited result from previous work.

claim: The alleles bearing isolated Forms 2 and 3 exhibited significant instabilities in the presence of Phen-DC3 but little to none in the absence of Pif1.
source: We also noted that the alleles bearing isolated Forms 2 and 3 exhibited significant instabilities in the presence of Phen-DC3 but little to none in the absence of Pif1 (Table 1 and Figure 5).
evidence: This is an observation based on the instability data in Table 1 and Figure 5.

claim: Phen-DC3 stabilized all forms, but to varying degrees.
source: Indeed, we found that Phen-DC3 stabilized all forms, but to varying degrees.
evidence: This is supported by CD-melting experiments comparing Tm with and without Phen-DC3.

claim: The ΔTm for Forms 1, 2 and 4 were similarly increased by 13.3°C to 17.7°C by Phen-DC3.
source: Namely the ΔTm for Forms 1, 2 and 4 were similarly increased by 13.3°C to 17.7°C
evidence: This is supported by CD-melting data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Form 3 exhibited a large ΔTm of +45.6°C upon Phen-DC3 treatment.
source: but Form 3 exhibited a large ΔTm of +45.6°C (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by CD-melting data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Form 1 and 3 reach a Tm of >80°C in the presence of Phen-DC3.
source: The consequence of this differential effect is that Form 1 and 3 now reach a Tm of >80°C
evidence: This is calculated from the Tm data with and without Phen-DC3.

claim: Form 2 and 4 have a Tm hovering at ~60°C in the presence of Phen-DC3.
source: while Form 2 and 4 have a Tm hovering at ~60°C.
evidence: This is calculated from the Tm data with and without Phen-DC3.

claim: The high level of G4-induced CEB1 instability correlated with the high thermal stability of the corresponding G4 in vitro.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that the high level of G4-induced CEB1 instability correlated with the high thermal stability of the corresponding G4 in vitro.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the correlation analysis between Tm and instability.

claim: Phen-DC3 differentially increases the Tm of the various G4s.
source: Importantly, it revealed that Phen-DC3 differentially increases the Tm of the various G4s, allowing explaining certain quantitative discrepancies observed in the WT+Phen-DC3 and pif1Δ contexts (see Discussion).
evidence: This is supported by the CD-melting data showing different ΔTm values for different forms.

claim: According to the G4 motif, G4-ligands have the potential to exacerbate effects of otherwise more labile non-canonical G4s.
source: Hence, according to the G4 motif, G4-ligands have the potential to exacerbate effects of otherwise more labile non-canonical G4s (Chambers et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential stabilization effects of Phen-DC3 and is supported by a citation.

claim: The discordant behavior of CEB1-G12T and CEB1-G(12,25)T suggests that the G12T mutation causes the formation of an uncharacterized new form that might be strongly stabilized by Phen-DC3.
source: In our case, the discordant behavior of CEB1-G12T and CEB1-G(12,25)T, which induces more instability that CEB1-WT in the Phen-DC3-treated context yet almost abolishes the instability in the Pif1-deficient context, suggests that the G12T mutation causes the formation of an uncharacterized new form that might be strongly stabilized by Phen-DC3.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the unusual behavior of the G12T mutant.

claim: A ChIP-Seq experiment using a G4-specific antibody identified only ~10,000 regions in human genomes, specifically enriched at nucleosome-depleted regions.
source: Indeed, a ChIP-Seq experiment using a G4-specific antibody identified only ~10,000 regions in human genomes, specifically enriched at nucleosome-depleted regions (Hänsel-Hertsch et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a cited result from a previous ChIP-Seq study.

claim: Only a subset of the potential G4 sequences are 'at risk' for genomic instability.
source: Similarly, our studies point at only a subset of the potential G4 sequences as being 'at risk' for genomic instability.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the structure-function analysis showing that not all G4-forming sequences cause instability.

claim: The innocuousness of other sequences could either be because G4 with longer loops did not form in vivo or because they failed to interfere with leading-strand replication.
source: The innocuousness of other sequences could either be because G4 with longer loops did not form in vivo or because they failed to interfere with leading-strand replication (Piazza et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for why some G4-forming sequences do not cause instability, supported by a citation.

claim: The complex in vivo situation argues against a 'one-fits-all' G4 prediction algorithm for genome data mining.
source: This complex in vivo situation, affected both by the local context such as nucleosome occupancy, the presence of G4-stabilizing ligands, and likely dependent of the biological processes under scrutiny, argues against a 'one-fits-all' G4 prediction algorithm for genome data mining.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the complexity of G4 behavior in vivo.

claim: The study identifies a subset of the most compact and stable canonical and non-canonical G4s that bears the biophysical properties required to form and hinder leading strand replication.
source: With regards to genomic instability, our study identifies a subset of the most compact and stable canonical and non-canonical G4s that bears the biophysical properties required to form and hinder leading strand replication.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study's findings.

claim: The structure-function analysis provides evidence for the existence of non-canonical G4s in vivo and their involvement in inducing high levels of genomic instability.
source: Hence, our structure-function analysis provides evidence for the existence of non-canonical G4s in vivo and their involvement in inducing high levels of genomic instability, as observed for the canonical CEB25-G4 motif composed of 4 G-triplets and loops of 1 nt (Piazza et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study's findings.

claim: A 0-nt loop was previously reported for the VEGF aptamer, although encompassing only 2 quartets.
source: Among the numerous structural studies of G4s, a 0-nt loop, such as in Form 3, were previously reported for the VEGF aptamer, although encompassing only 2 quartets (Marušič et al., 2013)
evidence: This is a cited structural observation from previous work.

claim: Snapback guanines occupying the vacant slot in outermost quartets were observed in the G4 of the c-MYC, c-KIT and PDGFRβ promoters.
source: snapback guanines occupying the vacant slot in outermost quartets such as in Form 1 were observed in the G4 of the c-MYC, c-KIT and PDGFRβ promoters (Phan et al., 2007, Phan et al., 2005)
evidence: This is a cited structural observation from previous work.

claim: The V-shaped loop associated with snapback guanines was reported for the CHL1 intronic G4.
source: and the associated V-shaped loop was reported for the CHL1 intronic G4 (Kuryavyi and Patel, 2010)
evidence: This is a cited structural observation from previous work.

claim: G-triads have been reported for synthetic model sequences and derivatives of the human MYOG G4.
source: Finally, G-triads such as in Form 2 have been reported for synthetic model sequences and derivatives of the human MYOG G4 (Heddi et al., 2016; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a cited structural observation from previous work.

claim: The vacant slot of a triad can be filled up by freely diffusing guanine derivatives.
source: Interestingly, in addition to nearby guanines, the vacant slot of a triad can be filled up by freely diffusing guanine derivatives (Park et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a cited observation from previous work.

claim: G-triad-containing G4s bear the unique property of being (deoxy)riboswitches sensitive to the abundance of guanine derivatives, which act as endogenous stabilizing ligands.
source: As previously proposed (Heddi et al., 2016; Li et al., 2015), G-triad-containing G4s bear the unique property of being (deoxy)riboswitches sensitive to the abundance of guanine derivatives, which act as endogenous stabilizing ligands.
evidence: This is a cited proposal about the functional properties of G-triad-containing G4s.

claim: The additivity for full CEB1 instability of the contributing Forms 2 and 3 in the presence of Phen-DC3, and of Form 1 with an unidentified form in the absence of Pif1, suggests the lack of interference or cooperation between forms in the array.
source: A noteworthy observation regards the additivity for full CEB1 instability of the contributing Forms 2 and 3 in the presence of Phen-DC3, and of Form 1 with an unidentified form in the absence of Pif1 (Figure 5B), suggesting the lack of interference or cooperation between forms in the array.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the quantitative analysis of instability contributions.

claim: The absence of competition between forms can be explained if each motif has an overall low propensity to fold into a G4 at the time required to interfere with replication.
source: This absence of competition can be explained if each motif has an overall low propensity to fold into a G4 at the time required to interfere with replication (Lopes et al., 2011), implying that G4 formation is a limiting step in CEB1 instability.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed additivity, supported by a citation.

claim: Loop sequence and G-tract proximity are determinants of G4-induced array genomic instability, in correlation with G4 thermal stability.
source: By systematically determining the thermal stability of motif variants, and by varying lengths and sequences of single purine loops involved in all forms (A19), we confirmed with the complex CEB1 sequence that loop sequence and G-tract proximity are determinants of G4-induced array genomic instability, in correlation with G4 thermal stability.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the systematic analysis of loop variants and their thermal stability.

claim: The correlation between Tm and instability was more robust in the pif1Δ than in the Phen-DC3-treated context.
source: This correlation was more robust in the pif1Δ than in the Phen-DC3-treated context (Figure 6A), due to notable deviations affecting Forms 2 and 3 upon Phen-DC3 treatment.
evidence: This is an observation based on the correlation analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Phen-DC3 is a universal G4 binder due to its recognition of an exposed G-quartet.
source: Phen-DC3 is a universal G4 binder due to its recognition of an exposed G-quartet (Chung et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a cited property of Phen-DC3.

claim: The disproportionately high stabilization of certain non-canonical G4 by Phen-DC3 likely results from the overcoming of the outmost quartet lability due to π-stacking interactions rather than from a differential G4 recognition.
source: Consequently, its disproportionately high stabilization of certain non-canonical G4 likely results from the overcoming of the outmost quartet lability (due to the 0-nt loop in Form 3 and the G-triad in Form 2) thanks to π-stacking interactions rather than from a differential G4 recognition.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation inferred from the structural properties of the forms and the known binding mode of Phen-DC3.

claim: Change in relative thermal stability induced by Phen-DC3 explains the discrepancies observed between the Phen-DC3 and the pif1Δ contexts for isolated forms.
source: Thus, change in relative thermal stability induced by Phen-DC3 explains the discrepancies observed between the Phen-DC3 and the pif1Δ contexts for isolated forms, whereby the most stable forms induce instability in both contexts.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential stabilization effects of Phen-DC3.

claim: The differences in G4 stabilization by Phen-DC3 were not revealed with the canonical CEB25 motif and variants because of their monomorphic structures, all evenly stabilized by Phen-DC3.
source: These differences were not revealed with the canonical CEB25 motif and variants because of their monomorphic structures, all evenly stabilized by Phen-DC3 (Piazza et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous work on CEB25, supported by a citation.

claim: A new generation of G4 prediction algorithms re-evaluated to ~700,000 the number of potential G4 sequences in the human genome.
source: As outlined in the Introduction, a new generation of G4 prediction algorithms that takes into account non-canonical G4s re-evaluated to ~700,000 the number of potential G4 sequences in the human genome (Bedrat et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a cited result from a previous computational study.

claim: The evidence for the existence of non-canonical G4s in cells revealed here gives relevance to the increased figure of ~700,000 potential G4 sequences.
source: The evidence for the existence of non-canonical G4s in cells revealed here gives relevance to this increased figure.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings about non-canonical G4s.

claim: How many of the potential G4 sequences actually form or exert a given biological function in cells remains uncertain.
source: However, how many of these potential G4 sequences actually form or exert a given biological function in cells remains uncertain.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The CEB1 motif is 77% GC-rich with a GC-skew of 77%.
source: The CEB1 motif (39 nt) is 77% GC-rich with a GC-skew of 77%.
evidence: This is a sequence composition analysis of the CEB1 motif.

claim: The CEB1 motif comprises seven G-tracts: one G-sextet (G9-14), three G-triplets (G2-4, G16-18 and G20-22) and three G-doublets (G24-25, G31-32, G34-35).
source: It comprises seven G-tracts: one G-sextet (G9-14), three G-triplets (G2-4, G16-18 and G20-22) and three G-doublets (G24-25, G31-32, G34-35) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a sequence analysis of the CEB1 motif shown in Figure 2A.
